case.caption: Menominee Tribe of Wis. v. United States

case_history.explanation: An official oral-argument transcript was verified.

case.dek: The Menominee Tribe seeks equitable tolling based on bad legal advice. The government opposes this exception.

revisions.correction_note: Rewritten to the concise citizen-facing editorial standard.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The Menominee Tribe of Wisconsin sued the United States. The tribe claims it missed the filing deadline. It relied on legal advice that it did not need to exhaust administrative remedies. The government argues the deadline is strict. The tribe argues the advice was reasonable. The lower court rejected the tribe's claim.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on December 1, 2015.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The tribe wants the Court to allow equitable tolling for erroneous legal advice.
The government wants the Court to enforce the strict filing deadline.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The tribe argues reasonable legal advice justifies tolling the deadline.
The government argues legal advice never justifies equitable tolling.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines when courts excuse missed deadlines. It affects how parties rely on legal counsel. It shapes the scope of equitable tolling doctrines. It impacts access to federal courts for tribal nations. It clarifies the role of administrative exhaustion requirements.
